summary:
Red Traverse is an interactive Marswalk planning prototype for Jezero Crater. It combines NASA/JPL orbital imagery, USGS terrain and geological mapping, and archived Perseverance tracks and surface observations in one browser interface. Users select science stops, set a maximum terrain grade, and compare routes that prioritize shorter distance or gentler slopes. The application calculates distance, cumulative climb, peak grid-scale slope, an elevation profile, and an illustrative round-trip time, then exports the route and stops as GeoJSON with Mars-specific metadata.

Our contribution is the integration of scientific destinations with explainable terrain-based route choices. NASA data drives the calculations as well as the visualization. Users can investigate how a planning decision changes the journey while retaining access to its sources and assumptions.

Red Traverse addresses the challenge through a working, localized, multi-mission planning workflow. It makes authentic planetary data accessible for education and exploration planning, while clearly distinguishing archived observations and model estimates from validated astronaut navigation.
details:
Purpose and connection to the challenge

Red Traverse explores how a future human explorer could choose science destinations and account for the terrain along the way. Jezero Crater provides a coherent scenario for investigating the crater floor and ancient delta, with archived Perseverance observations for context. The rover landing site and waypoints serve as reference locations for a hypothetical human traverse.

What the prototype does

Users can explore orbital imagery, derived slopes, and mapped geological units. A 3D Mars globe provides global orientation. The local planner offers expedition presets and supports up to six stops, including custom waypoints. Users set a maximum uphill or downhill grade and choose “Shorter walk” or “Gentler slopes.” The planner reports outbound distance, cumulative ascent, maximum modeled step slope, an elevation profile, and an illustrative round-trip duration.

Perseverance’s archived track and field notes connect the orbital map to rover photographs of the delta and Three Forks sample-depot area. The GeoJSON export contains the path, ordered stops, route metrics, grade limit, and route priority, with metadata identifying Mars and east-positive planetocentric coordinates.

How NASA data contributes

NASA/JPL Mars Trek supplies the MRO Context Camera basemap and the NASA/JPL–USGS Viking mosaic used on the globe. A USGS CTX terrain product with a nominal 20 m source grid supplies elevations for routing and the elevation profile. USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3464 supplies geological units. Archived NASA/JPL Mars 2020 tracks and waypoints anchor exploration context, and Perseverance images show terrain from the surface. Elevation affects the computed route. Geology and rover imagery help users interpret terrain and choose destinations.

Route method and assumptions

The planner uses A* search on an eight-neighbor elevation grid and visits stops in the selected order. “Shorter walk” uses horizontal grid distances as edge costs. “Gentler slopes” adds a quadratic penalty for steeper steps. Both modes exclude missing terrain cells and steps that exceed the selected grade limit. The time heuristic assumes an out-and-back walk on the same path, adjusts a selectable flat-ground pace for absolute grade, and adds 20 minutes per science stop after the start.

For “Delta reconnaissance” at an 18° limit and 2 km/h flat-ground pace, both routes display 2.79 km outbound. “Shorter walk” gives about 51 m of ascent, a 13.5° peak modeled slope, and a 3 h 37 min round trip. “Gentler slopes” gives about 33 m, 3.1°, and 3 h 32 min. These are prototype estimates.

Creativity and intended impact

Red Traverse connects the scientific reason for visiting a stop with the terrain needed to reach it. Students, educators, and space-exploration enthusiasts can compare route trade-offs, inspect assumptions, and explore real planetary data in one browser workflow. The prototype can support lessons on destination selection, terrain constraints, and the limits of orbital observations. A longer-term goal is a planning demonstrator for analogue exercises and human exploration studies.

Tools and implementation

The Vercel-hosted application uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules. Canvas renders the local map and elevation profile, and a custom renderer provides a WebGL globe with a fallback. Locally packaged elevation and geology grids support in-browser route recalculation. Design considerations included source resolution, missing terrain, coordinate conventions, attribution, grade limits, and keyboard interaction.

Limitations and next steps

The approximately 20 m terrain grid cannot resolve small rocks, cracks, or loose material. Geological boundaries reflect the source map’s scale. Three Forks is a nearby archived rover reference position. The prototype uses archived data and does not model live weather, dust, radiation, daylight, physiology, or suit resources. Next steps include higher-resolution obstacle checks, explicit uncertainty, validated resource constraints, and testing with users, independent route calculations, and domain experts.

Why the project merits recognition

Red Traverse demonstrates substantive use of NASA mission data in a working response to the challenge. It brings together a clear scientific setting, interactive route comparison, and traceable evidence. Its present value is accessible planetary-data exploration, with a clear path toward testing route calculations and planning assumptions.
